title: Meet the 2026 Ig Nobel Prize winners
gist: The 2026 Ig Nobel Prizes, moving permanently to European cities (Zurich this year, Antwerp next) because international winners and journalists are increasingly unwilling to travel to the US, honored offbeat but methodologically real research spanning splash-free urinal design, mosquito-proboscis 3D-printing nozzles, and evidence upper-class people behave less ethically.

themes.theme: Ceremony relocation reflects US travel reluctance

insights.claim: After 35 years in Boston, the Ig Nobel ceremony moved to Zurich, Switzerland in 2026 and will continue rotating through European cities for the foreseeable future, explicitly because international travelers have become increasingly reluctant to travel to the US.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A concrete, named data point (a 35-year US institution relocating abroad) evidencing declining international willingness to travel to the US — a soft indicator relevant to US inbound tourism, academic conference, and event-industry demand.
insights.quote: During the past year, it has become unsafe for our guests to visit the country
insights.locator: After 35 years in Boston, the annual prize ceremony

insights.claim: Four of the 2025 ceremony's 10 winners opted to skip the event rather than travel to the US, and organizer Marc Abrahams said the situation has not improved since, prompting the permanent move to Europe with Antwerp hosting next year and Zurich returning every even-numbered year from 2028 onward.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A 40% boycott rate among honorees in the prior year, followed by permanent relocation, is a concrete case study of reputational/safety concerns deterring international visitors and talent from engaging with US-based institutions.
insights.quote: We cannot in good conscience ask the new winners, or the international journalists who cover the event, to travel to the US this year.
insights.locator: "During the past year, it has become unsafe"

themes.theme: Notable award research with practical/technical relevance

insights.claim: A team won the Technology prize for developing 'necroprinting' — using a female mosquito's proboscis as a 3D-printing nozzle, achieving a print resolution of 18 to 22 microns, two times finer than the smallest commercially available metal dispensing tips, intended for future use printing scaffolds for living cells or microscopic electronic components.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A biologically-sourced nozzle achieving 2x the resolution of the best commercial metal tips is a genuine materials/manufacturing data point relevant to micro-fabrication and bio-printing research directions, despite its novelty framing.
insights.locator: The necroprinter achieved a resolution ranging from 18 to 22 microns

insights.claim: The Physics prize-winning 'Nautilus' splash-free urinal design, based on modeling how dogs angle their urine stream, achieves zero observed droplet splashback at an optimal 30-degree stream-to-surface angle, versus up to 50 times more splashback from conventional urinal designs.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A quantified engineering result (up to 50x splashback reduction) with direct commercial-design application potential (published in PNAS Nexus 2025) for plumbing fixture and hygiene product design.

insights.claim: The Economics prize went to researchers who found through seven studies that upper-class individuals (e.g., as measured by car type) were more likely to cut off other drivers and pedestrians, take candy meant for children, lie about dice-roll scores, and view greed as a positive attribute, concluding that self-interest pursuit is a more fundamental motive among society's elite.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Empirical, multi-study evidence linking socioeconomic status to unethical behavior patterns is relevant background for behavioral-economics and governance/ethics research applicable to corporate and elite decision-making studies.
insights.quote: the pursuit of self-interest is a more fundamental motive among society's elite
insights.locator: Again and again, the upper-class participants proved

insights.claim: The Chemistry prize-winning study found that milk protein crystals from viviparous cockroach (Diploptera punctata) embryos contain more than three times the energy of an equivalent amount of dairy milk, due to a tightly packed crystalline lattice structure enabling higher food-storage concentration.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A 3x energy-density-per-volume biomaterial discovery is a genuine data point of interest for novel nutrition/biomaterials research, despite the unusual source organism.
insights.quote: just one roach embryo crystal contained more than three times the energy of an equivalent amount of dairy milk

insights.claim: The Soil Science prize-winning citizen-science project buried 1,000 pairs of identical cotton underpants across more than 25 countries as an 'underpants index' for measuring soil decomposition rates and health, finding decomposition was fastest in private gardens (highest organic matter) and slowest in lawns, with results found to be as informative as the established 'teabag index.'
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Validates a low-cost, scalable citizen-science methodology (buried underwear) as comparably informative to an established scientific soil-health metric (teabag index), relevant for low-cost global agricultural/soil-monitoring approaches.
